extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter on indefinite and definite integrals, change of variable, and applications to areas (including parametric and polar forms) and volumes (slicing and revolution). Includes theorems, proofs, examples (ellipse, cycloid, lemniscate, torus), and sign/orientation conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of variable (substitution) in integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: When x = φ(t), a definite integral in x can be transformed into an integral in t: replace x by φ(t) and dx by φ'(t) dt; the two Riemann-sum representations have corresponding terms whose ratio tends to 1 as the mesh → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketched via Riemann sums: show termwise ratio tends to unity using derivative limit. The authors first assume φ' keeps a constant sign; if φ' does not have constant sign, divide the t-interval into subintervals where φ' has constant sign and apply the formula on each subinterval. When interchanging integration limits, change the sign of the integral. Examples: x = a cos t substitution to compute semi-ellipse area; many parametric examples use this rule to convert integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental theorem linking definite and indefinite integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: A definite integral is the difference of values of an antiderivative (integrale indefinie) at the endpoints: the definite integral equals the difference of the values of the indefinite integral for the two limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly in examples (ellipse, cycloid) to evaluate definite integrals once an antiderivative is found. When the antiderivative takes the same value at endpoints, its contribution is zero. Remember to account for sign when swapping limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a planar region via line integral ∫ y dx
rubrics_metrics.description: The area A of a planar region bounded by a simple closed curve can be expressed as the line integral A = ∮ y dx taken along the contour in the appropriate sense (text notes that the expression equals the integral taken on the contour in the sense of the arrow; the orientation sign matters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: moving a point along the contour, multiply its ordinate y by the projection dx of the small displacement; summing gives ∮ y dx. For practical calculation, parameterize the contour x(t), y(t) and compute ∫ y(t) x'(t) dt. For curves decomposable by vertical transversals, write area as difference of ∫ y_upper dx and ∫ y_lower dx. Examples include ellipse and foliium loop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientation and sign conventions for circulation and area
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive rotation is defined as that which brings Ox onto Oy (the usual trigonometric sense). Positive circulation of a closed contour is defined so that the radius vector O'M rotates by +2π when the mobile returns to initial position. The sign of integrals depends on the sense of traversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The area integral may be written with a − sign above the integral to indicate traversal in the negative sense (A = -∮ y dx). Reversing direction of traversal changes the sign of the integral, and integrals over arcs oriented opposite cancel appropriately. When a curve crosses an axis, the integral gives the algebraic difference between volumes/areas on each side. For curves with double points, the integral equals the sum/difference of areas of loops depending on orientation (examples and figures provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parametric formula for area (and volume) integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: If the coordinates of a point on the curve are given as functions x = x(t), y = y(t) where t runs from a to b and describes the curve once in the chosen sense, then integrals along the curve can be computed by substitution: ∮ y dx = ∫_a^b y(t) x'(t) dt (similarly for other integrands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard practical method to compute area and volume integrals for curves given parametrically (examples: cycloid, folium, ellipse parametrizations). Choose parameter interval so curve is traversed once in the appropriate sense; adjust limits/sign if traversal direction reversed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a closed curve via 1/2 ∮(x dy − y dx)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area A of a closed curve (without double points) can be given by the line integral A = (1/2) ∮ (x dy − y dx) taken along the curve in the positive sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formula is obtained by combining the sector and Cartesian-differential derivations. It is equivalent to the ∮ y dx expression with orientation bookkeeping. For curves with self-intersections, the same integral gives sum/difference of loop areas depending on configuration. Use parametric expressions to compute (x(t), y(t)) then integrate (1/2)(x x'_{?} − y y'_{?}) dt in practice (i.e., compute x(t) y'(t) − y(t) x'(t)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a sector in polar coordinates
rubrics_metrics.description: For a curve expressed in polar coordinates (r as function of θ), the differential of the sector area is dA = (1/2) r^2 dθ; hence A(θ) = (1/2) ∫ r(θ)^2 dθ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by sandwiching the infinitesimal sector between two circular sectors and letting Δθ → 0. Use this when the curve is naturally given by r(θ) (examples: lemniscate r^2 = a^2 cos 2θ). Remember to choose correct θ-interval corresponding to the desired sector or full curve, and the constant of integration is set by requiring area = 0 at starting angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential (element) of area in Cartesian coordinates (infinitesimal triangle/sector)
rubrics_metrics.description: The infinitesimal area element associated to a small displacement along a curve can be expressed via Cartesian differentials: for the small triangle/sector one gets an expression involving x and y differentials leading to the area-form used in the 1/2∮(x dy − y dx) formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive from the formula for area of triangle with vertex at origin: area = (1/2)(x1 y2 − x2 y1). For an infinitesimal sector OMM' with coordinates (x,y) and (x+dx,y+dy), the area element leads to the integrand x dy − y dx (up to the 1/2 and sign depending on orientation). Use this to switch between polar and Cartesian derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume of a solid with parallel bases by slicing
rubrics_metrics.description: If S(x) denotes the area of the cross-section of a solid by a plane perpendicular to axis Ox at abscissa x, then the differential of volume is dV = S(x) dx and the total volume is V = ∫_{x0}^{x1} S(x) dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by comparing the increment of volume to cylinders of base S and S' over small height Δx and letting Δx → 0. Works with possible geometric complications (projection of S onto other section partially outside) with slight modifications. Apply by computing S(x) via planar methods (areas previously developed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed-form formulas when S(x) is polynomial (esp. quadratic)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the cross-sectional area S(x) is a polynomial (notably quadratic) in x, one can integrate explicitly to get algebraic expressions for V. In particular, if S(x)=ax^2+bx+c on [0,h], then V integrates to a polynomial and can be expressed in terms of base areas S0, S1 and the middle section S_m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives a geometric interpretation and derives the formula V = (h/6)(S0 + S1 + 4 S_mid) when S is quadratic (where S_mid is area at x = h/2). Also notes this reduces to simpler expressions for lower-degree polynomials; verification exercises suggested. Apply to frustum of pyramid/cone, slice of sphere, ellipsoidal slices, paraboloid where S is linear (special case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplified volume formula when S(x) is linear
rubrics_metrics.description: If S(x) depends linearly on x (S(x) = α x + β), the volume between bases separated by h is V = (h/2)(S0 + S1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the special case of the polynomial formula; examples include slices of paraboloid where cross-sectional area varies linearly with x. Use midpoint/Simpson simplification appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume of revolution via line integral
rubrics_metrics.description: When rotating a planar region around Ox, the volume generated can be expressed as V = π ∮ y^2 dx taken along the boundary curve (with orientation/sign conventions determining whether it equals the difference of volumes when curve crosses the axis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a region bounded by an arc AMB that does not cross the axis, volume equals π ∫ y^2 dx (integral along that arc). If the curve crosses the axis, treat pieces separately and note that the integral yields algebraic difference of volumes generated by parts above and below the axis. Parametric computation: V = π ∫ y(t)^2 x'(t) dt over a traversal of the curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parametric computation of torus (illustrative example / Pappus application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute torus volume by parameterizing the generating circle: x = a + R cos t, y = R sin t, integrate V = π ∫ y^2 dx over 0..2π to obtain V = 2π^2 a R^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as an illustration of the general volume-of-revolution formula and of Guldin/Pappus theorem (volume = area × distance traveled by centroid). Also highlights handling of integrals where some terms integrate to zero by symmetry (cos and cos^3 over full period).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guldin's (Pappus) theorem relating centroid and volume
rubrics_metrics.description: When the centroid of a planar area is known, the volume generated by rotating that area around an axis in its plane equals the area multiplied by the distance traveled by its centroid during the rotation (i.e., area × 2π × (distance of centroid to axis)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text introduces this after deriving centers of gravity of plane areas; it provides a shortcut for volumes of revolution when centroid is available, avoiding direct integration. Useful for symmetric figures or where centroid is easy to compute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling curves with self-intersections (double points) in area/volume integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: If a closed curve has double points, the integral taken along the whole curve (∮ y dx or (1/2)∮(x dy − y dx)) represents either the difference or sum of the areas of the loops depending on the configuration; decomposition into loop contours and orientation analysis yields the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and figures (different dispositions) show how to split the contour into loops and how integrals over opposing arcs/straight segments cancel or add. Treat each loop separately as a closed contour with its own orientation; the algebraic sum gives the integral over the whole contour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of substitutions and parametrizations appropriate to the curve
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate area/volume integrals effectively, choose natural parametrizations or substitutions for the curve (e.g., x = a cos t for ellipse; cycloid parametric form x = a(t − sin t), y = a(1 − cos t); polar forms r(θ) for lemniscate or sectors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change variables carefully including limits and sign when reversing limits. Examples show interchanging limits and sign changes when convenient. Also exploit symmetry to eliminate integrals that vanish over symmetric intervals (cos terms over full period).
